final_rationale: The verdict does not change because the Actor introduced no new admissible evidence and mainly reframed the same record. That reframing is partly valid: the current evidence supports a narrower distinction between operational readiness and disclosure compliance. Aggregate readiness above threshold and no severity-one rehearsal incidents support readiness, and public NIST-style/model-card guidance supports monitoring and documentation as general controls. But the governing issue in this case is the specific internal policy requirement for a material limitation affecting a named launch use case. On the admissible record, the small-business onboarding segment misses target, is named in two paid pilot commitments, legal review is still open, and there is no evidence of required disclosure, resolution, or approved risk acceptance. That means the claim that certification can proceed on a readiness-and-monitoring basis remains unsupported under the cited policy. The concern is best understood as a bounded governance/disclosure failure rather than a general safety or launch-readiness failure, but it is still a compliance failure.
remaining_concerns: No admissible evidence shows approved risk acceptance for the specific small-business onboarding gap before launch.
No admissible evidence shows the limitation was disclosed in required launch or model-card materials.
Legal review remains open, so the materiality/disclosure predicate is unresolved on the current record.
The affected segment is named in two paid pilot commitments, which supports materiality under the stated policy text.
Aggregate readiness and a clean rehearsal support operational readiness but do not satisfy the separate internal disclosure requirement.
